[Surah al-Bayyinah]

It has eight verses and is Medinan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*) and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence: a Messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books. And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence: a Messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books. And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them.﴾

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

**Issue One:** Al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: "This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its composition and its exegesis, and the great scholars have stumbled over it. Moreover, may God have mercy on him, he did not clarify the nature of the difficulty in it." I say: The difficulty lies in this. The sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist [from their disbelief] until the clear evidence, which is the Messenger, came to them." Then He, exalted is He, did not mention what they were not going to desist from, but it is understood, since what is meant is the disbelief in which they were. So the sense becomes: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief until the clear evidence, which is the Messenger, came to them." Then the word *hatta* (until) indicates the end of a limit, so this verse implies that they would desist from their disbelief upon the arrival of the Messenger. Then He said afterwards: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾, and this implies that their disbelief increased upon the coming of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Thus there arises an apparent contradiction between the first verse and the second verse. This, as far as I think, is the extent of the difficulty.

The answer to it is from several aspects:

The first, and the best of them, is the aspect that the author of *al-Kashshaf* summarized: namely, that the disbelievers of both groups, the People of the Book and the idol-worshippers, used to say before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ): "We will not cease from what we are upon of our religion, nor will we abandon it until the awaited Prophet comes, who is written of in the Torah and the Gospel, and he is Muhammad, peace be upon him." So God related what they used to say, then said: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide﴾, meaning that they used to consider the unity of word and agreement upon the truth to be [a matter that would come] when the Messenger came to them. Then, what divided them from the truth and what kept them upon disbelief was only the coming of the Messenger. A parallel to this in speech is when a poor, sinful man says to one who admonishes him: "I will not refrain from the evil deeds I am engaged in until God grants me wealth." Then, when God grants him wealth, he increases in sin, and his admonisher says to him: "You were not free of sin until you became wealthy, and you did not plunge your head into sin except after you became affluent," reminding him of what he used to say, as a rebuke and a binding argument. The conclusion of this answer returns to one point, namely: His saying, "The disbelievers were not going to desist from their disbelief until the clear evidence came to them," is related as their own statement, and His saying, ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide﴾, is a report of what actually occurred. The meaning is that what happened was contrary to what they claimed.

The second: the sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief even if the clear evidence came to them." On this interpretation the difficulty disappears. This is how al-Qadi mentioned it, but interpreting the word *hatta* in this way is not in any way a matter of the language.

The third: We do not take His saying *munfakkin* (desisting) to refer to disbelief, but to their being detached from mentioning Muhammad with praiseworthy qualities and virtues. The meaning is: "Those who disbelieved were not detached from mentioning Muhammad with praiseworthy qualities and virtues until the clear evidence came to them." Ibn Arafah said: that is, "until it came to them," so the wording is in the present tense but the meaning is in the past, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what the devils recited﴾ (al-Baqarah, 102), meaning "what the devils had recited." The meaning is that they were not detached from mentioning his virtues, then when Muhammad came to them they divided concerning him, and each of them said about him a different, base statement. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (al-Baqarah, 89). The preferred view concerning this verse is the first.

There is a fourth aspect in the verse, which is that God judged the disbelievers to have not been detached from their disbelief until the time of the Messenger's coming. The word *hatta* implies that the state after that would be different from what it was before that. And so it was, because that gathered group did not remain upon disbelief; rather they divided, so some of them became believers and some of them became disbelievers. Since the state of that gathering did not remain after the Messenger's coming as it had been before his coming, this sufficed for the application of the implication of the word *hatta*.

There is a fifth aspect: that the disbelievers, before the mission of the Messenger, were not detached from firm conviction in their disbelief; rather they were resolute in it, holding its reality as true. Then that resolution disappeared after the Messenger's mission, and they remained doubting and bewildered regarding that religion and regarding all other religions. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community; then God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾ (al-Baqarah, 213). The meaning is that the religion they were upon had become, as it were, mixed into their flesh and blood. So the Jew was resolute in his Judaism, and likewise the Christian and the idol-worshipper. Then, when Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent, the thoughts and ideas were thrown into turmoil, and everyone doubted his religion, his creed and his doctrine. His saying, exalted is He, *munfakkin*, indicates this, because the detachment of one thing from another is its separation from it. So its meaning is that their hearts had not been empty of those beliefs and had not separated from firm conviction in their correctness. Then, after the mission, the matter did not remain in that state.

**Issue Two:** The disbelievers were of two kinds:

The first: the People of the Book, such as the sects of the Jews and the Christians, who were disbelievers because they introduced into their religion what they disbelieved in, such as their saying, "Ezra is the son of God" and "The Messiah is the son of God," and their distortion of the Book of God and His religion.

The second: the polytheists, who were not ascribed to any book. So God mentioned the two kinds by His saying, ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, in general terms, then followed that general statement with detail, which is His saying: ﴿among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾. Here there are two questions:

**First question:** The sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and among the polytheists." This implies that among the People of the Book some are disbelievers and some are not disbelievers, which is true; and that among the polytheists some are disbelievers and some are not disbelievers, which is clearly not true.

The answer is from several aspects:

First: the word *min* (among) here is not partitive but explanatory, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ (al-Hajj, 30).

Second: those who disbelieved in Muhammad, peace be upon him, were partly from the People of the Book and partly from the polytheists, so the word *min* was introduced for this reason.

Third: His saying, ﴿and the polytheists﴾, may also be a description of the People of the Book, because the Christians are Trinitarians and most of the Jews are anthropomorphists, and all of this is polytheism. A speaker may say: "The intelligent people and the witty people came to me," meaning a particular group whom he describes with both qualities. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who guard the limits of God﴾ (al-Tawbah, 112). This is a description of one single group. There is much of this type in the Qur'an, namely that a people is described with various attributes, some of which are joined to others by the conjunction *waw*, and the whole is a description of one single subject.

**Second question:** Are the Magians (Majus) included among the People of the Book? We say: Some scholars mentioned that they are included among the People of the Book, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "We shall treat them with the sunnah of the People of the Book." Others denied this, saying: Because God only mentioned among the disbelievers those who were in the land of the Arabs, namely the Jews and the Christians. God, exalted is He, said, relating their words: ﴿lest you say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾ (al-An'am, 156), and the two groups are the Jews and the Christians.

**Third question:** What is the benefit of mentioning the People of the Book before the polytheists in disbelief, where He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾? The answer: The conjunction *waw* does not indicate sequence, but nevertheless there are benefits in it:

First: the surah is Medinan, so it is as if the People of the Book were the primary intended subject of mention.

Second: they were scholars of the Scriptures, so their ability to recognize the truthfulness of Muhammad was more complete, and therefore their persistence in disbelief was more shameful.

Third: because they were scholars, others follow them, so their disbelief was the root of the disbelief of others, and for this reason they were mentioned first.

Fourth: because they were scholars, they were more noble than others, so they were mentioned first.

**Fourth question:** Why did He say *min Ahl al-Kitab* (among the People of the Book) and not *min al-Yahud wa al-Nasara* (among the Jews and the Christians)? The answer: Because His saying, ﴿among the People of the Book﴾, indicates that they were scholars, and this implies either greater honour, so they were mentioned with this title rather than as Jews and Christians; or because being a scholar implies greater ugliness in his disbelief, so they were mentioned with this description to draw attention to that additional increase in punishment.

**Issue Three:** This verse contains rulings related to the Sharia:

The first: God explained His saying, ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, as referring to the People of the Book and the polytheists. This implies that all of them are one in disbelief. On this basis the scholars said: "All disbelief is one religion (*milla*)." Therefore the polytheist inherits from the Jew and vice versa.

The second: the conjunction (*'atf*) necessitates difference, so for this reason we say: "The *dhimmi* (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection) is not a polytheist." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Not marrying their women and not eating their slaughtered animals," thereby establishing the distinction between the People of the Book and the polytheist.

The third: by mentioning the People of the Book, He alerted that it is not permissible to be deceived by the people of knowledge, since in the community of the Qur'an there has arisen something like what arose in the earlier nations.

**Issue Four:** Al-Qaffal said: *al-infikak* (desisting) is the separation of one thing from another, and its root is from *al-fakk*, which is opening and removal. From it comes "I unfastened the book," when I removed its seal and opened it. From it comes *fikak al-rahn* (redeeming the pledge), which is the removal of the bond that was upon it. Do you not see that the opposite of his saying "*infakka al-rahn*" (the pledge was released)... and from it comes *fikak al-asir* (ransoming the captive) and his release. Thus it is established that the separation of one thing from another is removing it after it has become attached to it, like a bone when it is dislocated from its joint. The meaning is that they were firmly clinging to their religion, a strong clinging that they would not remove except when the clear evidence came. As for *al-bayyinah* (clear evidence), it is the decisive proof by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. It is from *al-bayan* (clarification) or *al-bayunah* (distinction), because it clarifies the truth from falsehood. Concerning what is meant by *al-bayyinah* in this verse, there are several opinions:

The first: that it is the Messenger. Then they mentioned several reasons why the Messenger was called *al-bayyinah*:

The first: that his very person was a clear evidence of his prophethood. This is because he, peace be upon him, was in the utmost earnestness in establishing prophethood and messengership. Someone who is a liar and feigned cannot display that utmost earnestness. So nothing remains except that he was truthful or deranged.

The second is manifestly false, because he was in the utmost perfection of intellect. So nothing remains except that he was truthful.

The second: that the totality of the virtuous characteristics present in him reached the limit of miraculous perfection. Al-Jahiz established this meaning, and al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, supported it in *al-Munqidh*. So for these two reasons he himself was called a clear evidence.

**Part 2 of 2**

The third point: his (peace and blessings be upon him) miracles were extremely manifest and also extremely numerous. Because these two qualities were combined, he (peace be upon him) was in himself as though he were a clear proof and an argument. For this reason God Most High named him: ﴿a radiant lamp﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46]. Those who held that the meaning of "the clear proof" (al-bayyinah) is the Messenger argued from the words of God Most High after this verse: ﴿a messenger from God﴾. So it is in the nominative as an apposition (badal) to "the clear proof." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read it as "a messenger" (rasulan), as a circumstantial accusative (hal) of "the clear proof." They said: the alif and lam in His words ﴿the clear proof﴾ are for definiteness (ta'rif), meaning: he is the one whose mention preceded in the Torah and the Gospel through the tongues of Moses and Jesus. Or it may be said: they are for magnification (tafkhim), meaning: he is "the clear proof" beyond which there is nothing more, or "the clear proof" entire, because definiteness may be for magnification, and so may indefiniteness. God has combined both here regarding the Messenger (peace be upon him). He began with definiteness, which is the word "clear proof," then followed it with indefiniteness, saying: ﴿a messenger from God﴾, meaning: he is a messenger, and what a messenger! A parallel to this is what God Most High mentioned in praising Himself: ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious﴾ [al-Buruj: 15], then He said: ﴿Doer of what He intends﴾, so He used indefiniteness after definiteness.

The second view: the meaning of ﴿the clear proof﴾ is simply the messengers. This is the view of Abu Muslim, who said: the meaning of His words ﴿until there comes to them the clear proof﴾ is: until there come to them messengers from among God's angels, reciting to them purified scriptures (suhuf mutahharah). This is like His words: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and like His words: ﴿Rather, every one of them desires to be given open scrolls﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52].

The third view, which is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd: ﴿the clear proof﴾ is the Qur'an. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. Then His words after that: ﴿a messenger from God﴾ necessarily require an omitted modifier (mudaf mahdhuf), and the implied meaning is: that clear proof is a revelation, ﴿a messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures﴾.

As for His words, Most High: ﴿reciting purified scriptures, within which are upright books﴾, know that the suhuf are the plural of sahifah, which is a container for what is written. As for "purified" (al-mutahharah), there are several aspects:

First: purified (mutahharah) from falsehood. This is like His words: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42], and His words: ﴿exalted, purified﴾ [ʿAbasa: 14].

Second: purified from base mention, for the Qur'an is mentioned with the best of mention and is praised with the best of praise.

Third: it may be said: purified, meaning it should not be touched except by the purified (al-mutahharun), like His Most High words: ﴿in a hidden book, which none touches but the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 78–79].

Know that although "purified" is in grammatical agreement as an adjective to "scriptures" outwardly, it is in fact an adjective to what is in the scriptures, which is the Qur'an. As for His words ﴿books﴾, there are two opinions:

(One) The meaning of "books" is the verses written in the scriptures.

(Two) The author of al-Nazm said: "books" may carry the meaning of rulings, as in His words: ﴿God has decreed: "I will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21]. From this is the hadith of the hired laborer (al-asif): "By God, I will judge between you both by the Book of God," meaning by the ruling of God. So it is possible that the meaning of His words ﴿upright books﴾ is "upright rulings." As for "upright" (qayyimah), there are two opinions:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: it means straight, having no crookedness in it, distinguishing truth from falsehood, from the root qama, as in "sayyid" and "mayyit." This is like the saying: "the proof was established (qama) for such and such," meaning it became manifest and firm.

The second: "upright" (qayyimah) may mean "standing" (qa'imah), that is, it stands on its own, self-sufficient in argument and indication, from the saying: "so-and-so stood (qama) with the matter," meaning he carried it out properly. From this it is said of the one who manages the affairs of a people: "al-qayyim."

If it is asked: How is the recitation of the purified scriptures attributed to the Messenger, when he was unlettered (ummi)? We say: when he recited, for example, what was written in those scriptures, he was reciting what is in them. It has been reported in a book attributed to Jaʿfar al-Sadiq that he (peace be upon him) used to read from a book, although he did not write. Perhaps this was among his miracles (peace and blessings be upon him).

* * *

As for His words, Most High: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not split except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: there is a question regarding this verse. God Most High mentioned at the beginning of the surah the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) and the polytheists, and here He mentioned only the People of the Book. What is the reason for this? Its answer has several aspects:

One: the polytheists were not allowed to remain upon their religion, so whoever believed is intended, and whoever did not believe was killed. This is unlike the People of the Book, who are allowed to remain upon their disbelief by paying the jizyah (poll tax).

Two: the People of the Book had knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him) because they found it in their books. So when they are described as splitting despite knowledge, one who has no scripture is more fitting to be included under this description.

The second issue: al-Jubba'i said: this verse refutes the words of the Qadariyya (Qadariyyah, the early group who affirmed human power over actions) who said that people split into wretchedness and happiness in the loins of their fathers before the clear proof came to them. The answer is: this is weak, because what is meant by it is that God's knowledge of that and His will for it exist from eternity; as for its manifestation from the responsible person, it occurs only after the specific state.

The third issue: they said: this verse indicates that disbelief and splitting are their own act, not something decreed upon them. For He said: ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, then He said: ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, meaning God and His angels gave them that. So good and divine success are attributed to God, while evil, splitting and disbelief are attributed to them.

The fourth issue: the purpose of this verse is to console the Messenger (peace be upon him), meaning: let not their splitting grieve you, for it is not due to a deficiency in the proof but to their obstinacy. Their predecessors were likewise; they did not split over the Sabbath and the worship of the calf, ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾. So it is an ancient custom of theirs.

It has eight verses and is Medinan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

The sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist [from their disbelief] until the clear evidence, which is the Messenger, came to them." Then He, exalted is He, did not mention what they were not going to desist from, but it is understood, since what is meant is the disbelief in which they were. So the sense becomes: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief until the clear evidence, which is the Messenger, came to them." Then the word *hatta* (until) indicates the end of a limit, so this verse implies that they would desist from their disbelief upon the arrival of the Messenger. Then He said afterwards: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾, and this implies that their disbelief increased upon the coming of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Thus there arises an apparent contradiction between the first verse and the second verse. This, as far as I think, is the extent of the difficulty.

The answer to it is from several aspects:

The first, and the best of them, is the aspect that the author of *al-Kashshaf* summarized: namely, that the disbelievers of both groups, the People of the Book and the idol-worshippers, used to say before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ): "We will not cease from what we are upon of our religion, nor will we abandon it until the awaited Prophet comes, who is written of in the Torah and the Gospel, and he is Muhammad, peace be upon him." Then, what divided them from the truth and what kept them upon disbelief was only the coming of the Messenger. A parallel to this in speech is when a poor, sinful man says to one who admonishes him: "I will not refrain from the evil deeds I am engaged in until God grants me wealth." Then, when God grants him wealth, he increases in sin, and his admonisher says to him: "You were not free of sin until you became wealthy, and you did not plunge your head into sin except after you became affluent," reminding him of what he used to say, as a rebuke and a binding argument. The conclusion of this answer returns to one point, namely: His saying, "The disbelievers were not going to desist from their disbelief until the clear evidence came to them," is related as their own statement, and His saying, ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide﴾, is a report of what actually occurred. The meaning is that what happened was contrary to what they claimed.

The second: the sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief even if the clear evidence came to them." On this interpretation the difficulty disappears. This is how al-Qadi mentioned it, but interpreting the word *hatta* in this way is not in any way a matter of the language.

The third: We do not take His saying *munfakkin* (desisting) to refer to disbelief, but to their being detached from mentioning Muhammad with praiseworthy qualities and virtues. The meaning is: "Those who disbelieved were not detached from mentioning Muhammad with praiseworthy qualities and virtues until the clear evidence came to them." Ibn Arafah said: that is, "until it came to them," so the wording is in the present tense but the meaning is in the past, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what the devils recited﴾ (al-Baqarah, 102), meaning "what the devils had recited." The meaning is that they were not detached from mentioning his virtues, then when Muhammad came to them they divided concerning him, and each of them said about him a different, base statement. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (al-Baqarah, 89). The preferred view concerning this verse is the first.

There is a fourth aspect in the verse, which is that God judged the disbelievers to have not been detached from their disbelief until the time of the Messenger's coming. The word *hatta* implies that the state after that would be different from what it was before that. And so it was, because that gathered group did not remain upon disbelief; rather they divided, so some of them became believers and some of them became disbelievers. Since the state of that gathering did not remain after the Messenger's coming as it had been before his coming, this sufficed for the application of the implication of the word *hatta*.

His saying, exalted is He, *munfakkin*, indicates this, because the detachment of one thing from another is its separation from it. So its meaning is that their hearts had not been empty of those beliefs and had not separated from firm conviction in their correctness. As for His words, Most High: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not split except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: there is a question regarding this verse. God Most High mentioned at the beginning of the surah the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) and the polytheists, and here He mentioned only the People of the Book. What is the reason for this? Its answer has several aspects:

One: the polytheists were not allowed to remain upon their religion, so whoever believed is intended, and whoever did not believe was killed. This is unlike the People of the Book, who are allowed to remain upon their disbelief by paying the jizyah (poll tax).

Two: the People of the Book had knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him) because they found it in their books. So when they are described as splitting despite knowledge, one who has no scripture is more fitting to be included under this description.

The second issue: al-Jubba'i said: this verse refutes the words of the Qadariyya (Qadariyyah, the early group who affirmed human power over actions) who said that people split into wretchedness and happiness in the loins of their fathers before the clear proof came to them. The answer is: this is weak, because what is meant by it is that God's knowledge of that and His will for it exist from eternity; as for its manifestation from the responsible person, it occurs only after the specific state.

The third issue: they said: this verse indicates that disbelief and splitting are their own act, not something decreed upon them. For He said: ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, then He said: ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, meaning God and His angels gave them that. So good and divine success are attributed to God, while evil, splitting and disbelief are attributed to them.

The fourth issue: the purpose of this verse is to console the Messenger (peace be upon him), meaning: let not their splitting grieve you, for it is not due to a deficiency in the proof but to their obstinacy. Their predecessors were likewise; they did not split over the Sabbath and the worship of the calf, ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾. So it is an ancient custom of theirs.

[p. 37]

[Surah al-Bayyinah]

It has eight verses and is Medinan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*) and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence: a Messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books. And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence: a Messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures, in which are upright books. And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them.﴾

Know that there are several issues concerning this verse.

**Issue One:** Al-Wahidi said in *al-Basit*: "This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its composition and its exegesis, and the great scholars have stumbled over it. Moreover, may God have mercy on him, he did not clarify the nature of the difficulty in it." I say: The difficulty lies in this. The sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist [from their disbelief] until the clear evidence, which is the Messenger, came to them." Then He, exalted is He, did not mention what they were not going to desist from, but it is understood, since what is meant is the disbelief in which they were. So the sense becomes: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief until the clear evidence, which is the Messenger, came to them." Then the word *hatta* (until) indicates the end of a limit, so this verse implies that they would desist from their disbelief upon the arrival of the Messenger. Then He said afterwards: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾, and this implies that their disbelief increased upon the coming of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Thus there arises an apparent contradiction between the first verse and the second verse. This, as far as I think, is the extent of the difficulty.

The answer to it is from several aspects:

The first, and the best of them, is the aspect that the author of *al-Kashshaf* summarized: namely, that the disbelievers of both groups, the People of the Book and the idol-worshippers, used to say before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ): "We will not cease from what we are upon of our religion, nor will we abandon it until the awaited Prophet comes, who is written of in the Torah and the Gospel, and he is Muhammad, peace be upon him." So God related what they used to say, then said: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide﴾, meaning that they used to consider the unity of word and agreement upon the truth to be [a matter that would come] when the Messenger came to them. Then, what divided them from the truth and what kept them upon disbelief was only the coming of the Messenger. A parallel to this in speech is when a poor, sinful man says to one who admonishes him: "I will not refrain from the evil deeds I am engaged in until God grants me wealth." Then, when God grants him wealth, he increases in sin, and his admonisher says to him: "You were not free of sin until you became wealthy, and you did not plunge your head into sin except after you became affluent," reminding him of what he used to say, as a rebuke and a binding argument. The conclusion of this answer returns to one point, namely: His saying, "The disbelievers were not going to desist from their disbelief until the clear evidence came to them," is related as their own statement, and His saying, ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide﴾, is a report of what actually occurred. The meaning is that what happened was contrary to what they claimed.

The second: the sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief even if the clear evidence came to them." On this interpretation the difficulty disappears. This is how al-Qadi mentioned it, but interpreting the word *hatta* in this way is not in any way a matter of the language.

The third: We do not take His saying *munfakkin* (desisting) to refer to disbelief, but to their being detached from mentioning Muhammad with praiseworthy qualities and virtues. The meaning is: "Those who disbelieved were not detached from mentioning Muhammad with praiseworthy qualities and virtues until the clear evidence came to them." Ibn Arafah said: that is, "until it came to them," so the wording is in the present tense but the meaning is in the past, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿what the devils recited﴾ (al-Baqarah, 102), meaning "what the devils had recited." The meaning is that they were not detached from mentioning his virtues, then when Muhammad came to them they divided concerning him, and each of them said about him a different, base statement. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (al-Baqarah, 89). The preferred view concerning this verse is the first.

There is a fourth aspect in the verse, which is that God judged the disbelievers to have not been detached from their disbelief until the time of the Messenger's coming. The word *hatta* implies that the state after that would be different from what it was before that. And so it was, because that gathered group did not remain upon disbelief; rather they divided, so some of them became believers and some of them became disbelievers. Since the state of that gathering did not remain after the Messenger's coming as it had been before his coming, this sufficed for the application of the implication of the word *hatta*.

There is a fifth aspect: that the disbelievers, before the mission of the Messenger, were not detached from firm conviction in their disbelief; rather they were resolute in it, holding its reality as true. Then that resolution disappeared after the Messenger's mission, and they remained doubting and bewildered regarding that religion and regarding all other religions. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community; then God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾ (al-Baqarah, 213). The meaning is that the religion they were upon had become, as it were, mixed into their flesh and blood. So the Jew was resolute in his Judaism, and likewise the Christian and the idol-worshipper. Then, when Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent, the thoughts and ideas were thrown into turmoil, and everyone doubted his religion, his creed and his doctrine. His saying, exalted is He, *munfakkin*, indicates this, because the detachment of one thing from another is its separation from it. So its meaning is that their hearts had not been empty of those beliefs and had not separated from firm conviction in their correctness. Then, after the mission, the matter did not remain in that state.

* * *

**Issue Two:** The disbelievers were of two kinds:

The first: the People of the Book, such as the sects of the Jews and the Christians, who were disbelievers because they introduced into their religion what they disbelieved in, such as their saying, "Ezra is the son of God" and "The Messiah is the son of God," and their distortion of the Book of God and His religion.

The second: the polytheists, who were not ascribed to any book. So God mentioned the two kinds by His saying, ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, in general terms, then followed that general statement with detail, which is His saying: ﴿among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾. Here there are two questions:

**First question:** The sense of the verse is: "Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and among the polytheists." This implies that among the People of the Book some are disbelievers and some are not disbelievers, which is true; and that among the polytheists some are disbelievers and some are not disbelievers, which is clearly not true.

The answer is from several aspects:

First: the word *min* (among) here is not partitive but explanatory, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ (al-Hajj, 30).

Second: those who disbelieved in Muhammad, peace be upon him, were partly from the People of the Book and partly from the polytheists, so the word *min* was introduced for this reason.

Third: His saying, ﴿and the polytheists﴾, may also be a description of the People of the Book, because the Christians are Trinitarians and most of the Jews are anthropomorphists, and all of this is polytheism. A speaker may say: "The intelligent people and the witty people came to me," meaning a particular group whom he describes with both qualities. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin right and forbid wrong, and those who guard the limits of God﴾ (al-Tawbah, 112). This is a description of one single group. There is much of this type in the Qur'an, namely that a people is described with various attributes, some of which are joined to others by the conjunction *waw*, and the whole is a description of one single subject.

**Second question:** Are the Magians (Majus) included among the People of the Book? We say: Some scholars mentioned that they are included among the People of the Book, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "We shall treat them with the sunnah of the People of the Book." Others denied this, saying: Because God only mentioned among the disbelievers those who were in the land of the Arabs, namely the Jews and the Christians. God, exalted is He, said, relating their words: ﴿lest you say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾ (al-An'am, 156), and the two groups are the Jews and the Christians.

**Third question:** What is the benefit of mentioning the People of the Book before the polytheists in disbelief, where He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾? The answer: The conjunction *waw* does not indicate sequence, but nevertheless there are benefits in it:

First: the surah is Medinan, so it is as if the People of the Book were the primary intended subject of mention.

Second: they were scholars of the Scriptures, so their ability to recognize the truthfulness of Muhammad was more complete, and therefore their persistence in disbelief was more shameful.

Third: because they were scholars, others follow them, so their disbelief was the root of the disbelief of others, and for this reason they were mentioned first.

Fourth: because they were scholars, they were more noble than others, so they were mentioned first.

**Fourth question:** Why did He say *min Ahl al-Kitab* (among the People of the Book) and not *min al-Yahud wa al-Nasara* (among the Jews and the Christians)? The answer: Because His saying, ﴿among the People of the Book﴾, indicates that they were scholars, and this implies either greater honour, so they were mentioned with this title rather than as Jews and Christians; or because being a scholar implies greater ugliness in his disbelief, so they were mentioned with this description to draw attention to that additional increase in punishment.

* * *

**Issue Three:** This verse contains rulings related to the Sharia:

The first: God explained His saying, ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, as referring to the People of the Book and the polytheists. This implies that all of them are one in disbelief. On this basis the scholars said: "All disbelief is one religion (*milla*)." Therefore the polytheist inherits from the Jew and vice versa.

The second: the conjunction (*'atf*) necessitates difference, so for this reason we say: "The *dhimmi* (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection) is not a polytheist." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Not marrying their women and not eating their slaughtered animals," thereby establishing the distinction between the People of the Book and the polytheist.

The third: by mentioning the People of the Book, He alerted that it is not permissible to be deceived by the people of knowledge, since in the community of the Qur'an there has arisen something like what arose in the earlier nations.

* * *

**Issue Four:** Al-Qaffal said: *al-infikak* (desisting) is the separation of one thing from another, and its root is from *al-fakk*, which is opening and removal. From it comes "I unfastened the book," when I removed its seal and opened it. From it comes *fikak al-rahn* (redeeming the pledge), which is the removal of the bond that was upon it. Do you not see that the opposite of his saying "*infakka al-rahn*" (the pledge was released)... and from it comes *fikak al-asir* (ransoming the captive) and his release. Thus it is established that the separation of one thing from another is removing it after it has become attached to it, like a bone when it is dislocated from its joint. The meaning is that they were firmly clinging to their religion, a strong clinging that they would not remove except when the clear evidence came. As for *al-bayyinah* (clear evidence), it is the decisive proof by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. It is from *al-bayan* (clarification) or *al-bayunah* (distinction), because it clarifies the truth from falsehood. Concerning what is meant by *al-bayyinah* in this verse, there are several opinions:

The first: that it is the Messenger. Then they mentioned several reasons why the Messenger was called *al-bayyinah*:

The first: that his very person was a clear evidence of his prophethood. This is because he, peace be upon him, was in the utmost earnestness in establishing prophethood and messengership. Someone who is a liar and feigned cannot display that utmost earnestness. So nothing remains except that he was truthful or deranged.

The second is manifestly false, because he was in the utmost perfection of intellect. So nothing remains except that he was truthful.

The second: that the totality of the virtuous characteristics present in him reached the limit of miraculous perfection. Al-Jahiz established this meaning, and al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, supported it in *al-Munqidh*. So for these two reasons he himself was called a clear evidence.

**Part 2 of 2**

The third point: his (peace and blessings be upon him) miracles were extremely manifest and also extremely numerous. Because these two qualities were combined, he (peace be upon him) was in himself as though he were a clear proof and an argument. For this reason God Most High named him: ﴿a radiant lamp﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46]. Those who held that the meaning of "the clear proof" (al-bayyinah) is the Messenger argued from the words of God Most High after this verse: ﴿a messenger from God﴾. So it is in the nominative as an apposition (badal) to "the clear proof." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read it as "a messenger" (rasulan), as a circumstantial accusative (hal) of "the clear proof." They said: the alif and lam in His words ﴿the clear proof﴾ are for definiteness (ta'rif), meaning: he is the one whose mention preceded in the Torah and the Gospel through the tongues of Moses and Jesus. Or it may be said: they are for magnification (tafkhim), meaning: he is "the clear proof" beyond which there is nothing more, or "the clear proof" entire, because definiteness may be for magnification, and so may indefiniteness. God has combined both here regarding the Messenger (peace be upon him). He began with definiteness, which is the word "clear proof," then followed it with indefiniteness, saying: ﴿a messenger from God﴾, meaning: he is a messenger, and what a messenger! A parallel to this is what God Most High mentioned in praising Himself: ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious﴾ [al-Buruj: 15], then He said: ﴿Doer of what He intends﴾, so He used indefiniteness after definiteness.

The second view: the meaning of ﴿the clear proof﴾ is simply the messengers. This is the view of Abu Muslim, who said: the meaning of His words ﴿until there comes to them the clear proof﴾ is: until there come to them messengers from among God's angels, reciting to them purified scriptures (suhuf mutahharah). This is like His words: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], and like His words: ﴿Rather, every one of them desires to be given open scrolls﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 52].

The third view, which is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd: ﴿the clear proof﴾ is the Qur'an. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. Then His words after that: ﴿a messenger from God﴾ necessarily require an omitted modifier (mudaf mahdhuf), and the implied meaning is: that clear proof is a revelation, ﴿a messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures﴾.

As for His words, Most High: ﴿reciting purified scriptures, within which are upright books﴾, know that the suhuf are the plural of sahifah, which is a container for what is written. As for "purified" (al-mutahharah), there are several aspects:

First: purified (mutahharah) from falsehood. This is like His words: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42], and His words: ﴿exalted, purified﴾ [ʿAbasa: 14].

Second: purified from base mention, for the Qur'an is mentioned with the best of mention and is praised with the best of praise.

Third: it may be said: purified, meaning it should not be touched except by the purified (al-mutahharun), like His Most High words: ﴿in a hidden book, which none touches but the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 78–79].

[p. 41]

Know that although "purified" is in grammatical agreement as an adjective to "scriptures" outwardly, it is in fact an adjective to what is in the scriptures, which is the Qur'an. As for His words ﴿books﴾, there are two opinions:

(One) The meaning of "books" is the verses written in the scriptures.

(Two) The author of al-Nazm said: "books" may carry the meaning of rulings, as in His words: ﴿God has decreed: "I will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21]. From this is the hadith of the hired laborer (al-asif): "By God, I will judge between you both by the Book of God," meaning by the ruling of God. So it is possible that the meaning of His words ﴿upright books﴾ is "upright rulings." As for "upright" (qayyimah), there are two opinions:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: it means straight, having no crookedness in it, distinguishing truth from falsehood, from the root qama, as in "sayyid" and "mayyit." This is like the saying: "the proof was established (qama) for such and such," meaning it became manifest and firm.

The second: "upright" (qayyimah) may mean "standing" (qa'imah), that is, it stands on its own, self-sufficient in argument and indication, from the saying: "so-and-so stood (qama) with the matter," meaning he carried it out properly. From this it is said of the one who manages the affairs of a people: "al-qayyim."

If it is asked: How is the recitation of the purified scriptures attributed to the Messenger, when he was unlettered (ummi)? We say: when he recited, for example, what was written in those scriptures, he was reciting what is in them. It has been reported in a book attributed to Jaʿfar al-Sadiq that he (peace be upon him) used to read from a book, although he did not write. Perhaps this was among his miracles (peace and blessings be upon him).

* * *

As for His words, Most High: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not split except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: there is a question regarding this verse. God Most High mentioned at the beginning of the surah the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) and the polytheists, and here He mentioned only the People of the Book. What is the reason for this? Its answer has several aspects:

One: the polytheists were not allowed to remain upon their religion, so whoever believed is intended, and whoever did not believe was killed. This is unlike the People of the Book, who are allowed to remain upon their disbelief by paying the jizyah (poll tax).

Two: the People of the Book had knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him) because they found it in their books. So when they are described as splitting despite knowledge, one who has no scripture is more fitting to be included under this description.

The second issue: al-Jubba'i said: this verse refutes the words of the Qadariyya (Qadariyyah, the early group who affirmed human power over actions) who said that people split into wretchedness and happiness in the loins of their fathers before the clear proof came to them. The answer is: this is weak, because what is meant by it is that God's knowledge of that and His will for it exist from eternity; as for its manifestation from the responsible person, it occurs only after the specific state.

The third issue: they said: this verse indicates that disbelief and splitting are their own act, not something decreed upon them. For He said: ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, then He said: ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, meaning God and His angels gave them that. So good and divine success are attributed to God, while evil, splitting and disbelief are attributed to them.

The fourth issue: the purpose of this verse is to console the Messenger (peace be upon him), meaning: let not their splitting grieve you, for it is not due to a deficiency in the proof but to their obstinacy. Their predecessors were likewise; they did not split over the Sabbath and the worship of the calf, ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾. So it is an ancient custom of theirs.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth, and to establish prayer and give zakah. And that is the upright religion﴾. And in this there are several issues:

[Page 42]

The first issue: Concerning His saying ﴿And they were not commanded﴾, there are two possibilities:

The first: that what is meant is: "And they were not commanded in the Torah and the Gospel except with the upright monotheistic religion (al-din al-hanifi)." Thus the meaning is that they were commanded with this, except that when He, exalted, followed it with His saying ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾, we know that just as this ruling was prescribed for them, it is prescribed for us as well.

The second: that what is meant is: "And the People of the Book were not commanded, through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ), except with these things." This is preferable, for three reasons:

The first: that the verse on this reading conveys a new law, and interpreting the speech of Allah in the way that yields greater benefit is preferable.

The second: that the mention of Muhammad, peace be upon him, has already occurred here, in His saying ﴿until there came to them clear evidence﴾, whereas the mention of the other prophets, peace be upon them, has not preceded.

The third: that He, exalted, concluded the verse with His saying ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾, thereby ruling that what is the subject of this verse is an upright religion, so it must be a law for us, whether we say it is the law of those before us or a new law which this serves as an elucidation of the law of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. This is the view of Muqatil.

The second issue: Concerning His saying ﴿to worship Allah﴾, there is a subtle point: this lam is the lam of purpose (lam al-gharad), so it cannot be taken in its apparent sense, because whoever does an act for a purpose is deficient in essence and completed by that purpose. Thus if God performed an act, He would be deficient in essence and completed by something other than Himself, which is impossible. For if that purpose is eternal, the eternity of the act necessarily follows from its eternity; and if it is originated, it requires another purpose, and so there follows an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Moreover, if He were unable to achieve that purpose except through that intermediary, then He would be incapable; and if He were able to achieve it, then introducing that intermediary would be pointless. Thus it is established that it cannot be taken in its apparent sense, and so interpretation (ta'wil) is necessary.

Then al-Farra' said: The Arabs often use the lam in place of "an" with commands and desires. Among that is His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], ﴿They desire to extinguish﴾ [al-Saff: 8]. And He said regarding a command: ﴿And we were commanded to submit﴾ [al-An'am: 71]. And in the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "And they were not commanded except that they worship Allah." Thus it is established that the meaning is: "And they were not commanded except that they worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion." Sincerity (al-ikhlas) is an expression for pure intention (al-niyyah al-khalisah). Since pure intention is taken into account, intention itself is taken into account. Thus the verse indicates that every thing commanded must be intended. Then the Shafi'is said: ablution is commanded in His saying ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and this verse indicates that every commanded act must be intended; so from the combination of the two verses it follows that ablution must be intended. As for the Mu'tazilah, they hold that the acts and rulings of Allah are causally explained by purposes; therefore they took the verse in its apparent sense and said the meaning is: "They were not commanded with anything except for the sake of worshipping Allah," and the argument for this view is also strong, since the sense is: "They were not commanded with anything except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion in that thing." This too requires taking intention into account for all commanded acts. If it is said: reflection upon knowledge of Allah is commanded, and it is impossible to take intention into account in it, since intention cannot be considered except after knowledge, so what precedes knowledge cannot have intention taken into account — we say: suppose that the general wording is specified in this case by the rational proof you have mentioned; the remainder remains a valid proof.

* * *

The third issue: His saying ﴿they were commanded﴾ is stated in the passive form, like ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] and ﴿Retaliation has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. They said: there are several explanations for this:

The first: it is as if He, exalted, says: worship is burdensome, and I do not desire your hardship as a primary desire; rather My desire for your worship is like a mother's desire for your cupping. For this reason, when the matter returned to mercy, He said: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 54], ﴿He has written faith in their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]. It is mentioned in the accounts that when a father wishes his son to do a deed, he first says: "It would be fitting for you to do this," and does not command him explicitly, because he may refuse, and then his offense would be great. Likewise here, He did not state the command explicitly, so that the offense of the one who refuses would be lightened.

The second: that we, on the premise of rational good and evil, say: it is as if He, exalted, says: I am not the sole one who commands worship; your intellect also commands you, because the utmost in honouring the one who has bestowed favour upon you is obligatory according to the intellects.

The fourth issue: The lam in His saying ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah﴾ indicates the position of the People of the Sunnah, who said: worship is not obligatory because it leads to the reward of Paradise or to distance from the punishment of Hell, but rather because you are a servant and He is the Lord. Even if there were no reward or punishment at all in religion, He would still have commanded you to worship, and it would be obligatory purely for the sake of servitude. There is also in this an indication that whoever worships Allah for reward and punishment, then in reality what he worships is the reward and punishment, and the Truth is merely an intermediary. And how well it has been said: "Whoever prefers knowing for the sake of knowing has spoken the second [truth]; but whoever prefers knowing not for the sake of knowing, but for the sake of the Known, has plunged into the depths of arrival."

The fifth issue: Worship ('ibadah) is humbling oneself (al-tadhallul); from it comes "a paved road" (tariq mu'abbad), i.e., made smooth. Whoever claims it is obedience has erred, for a group worshipped the angels, the Messiah and idols, and they did not obey them. But in the Sharia it became a term for every act of obedience to Allah performed in a manner of humility and utmost veneration. Know that worship in this sense is deserved only by one who is unique in his essence and in his essential and active attributes; if there were a like, it would not be permissible to direct to him the utmost veneration. Then we say: for an act to be worship, two things are necessary:

The first: the utmost veneration. For this reason we say that the prayer of a child is not worship, because he does not know the greatness of Allah, so his act does not reach the utmost veneration.

The second: that it be commanded. Thus the act of a Jew is not worship, even if it includes utmost veneration, because he is not commanded with it. The admonitory point here is that the child's act is not worship due to the absence of veneration, and the Jew's act is not worship due to the absence of command. So how could your deficient bowing be worship when there is neither command nor veneration?

* * *

The sixth issue: Sincerity (ikhlas) is to perform the act purely for one single motive, with no other motives having influence in calling one to that act. Its admonitory points are of several kinds:

The first: it is as if He, exalted, says: My servant, do not strive to increase obedience, but rather to purify it. For I did not give you all My capacity so that I would demand from you all of your capacity; rather I gave you a portion, so I demand from you a portion: half of twenty, and a sheep out of forty. But the portion I performed, I did not intend by its performance anyone other than you; so do not intend by your obedience anyone other than Me. Do not reserve for yourself a share of your obedience, let alone reserve it for another. So the permissible matter that occurs from you in prayer, such as scratching or clearing the throat, is a share you have reserved for yourself, and thus sincerity is lost; as for the disliked turning of attention, that is the portion of Satan.

The second: it is as if He, exalted, said: O intellect, you are wise, you do not incline to ignorance and folly, and I am wise and I do not do that at all. Therefore you should not desire except what I desire, and I do not desire except what you desire. Furthermore, He, glorified is He, is King of the worlds, and the intellect is king of this body. So it is as if He, exalted, by His grace said: A king does not serve a king; but so that we may come to agreement, I make all that I do for your sake: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. So you too make all that you do for My sake: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿sincere﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and it is an indication of what is required of attaining sincerity from the beginning of the act to its end. The sincere one is he who performs the good because it is good, and the obligatory because it is obligatory, so he performs the act for its own sake, sincere to his Lord, not desiring showing-off (riya'), nor reputation (sum'ah), nor any other aim. Rather they said: the attainment of Paradise should not be made the object of intent, nor deliverance from Hell the sought goal, even though this is necessary in some sense. In the Torah it is said: "What is done for My face, its little is much, and what is done for other than My face, its much is little." They also said that among sincerity is that one does not add to acts of worship another act of worship for the sake of others. For example, the obligatory sacrifice is a sheep; if you slaughter two, one for Allah and one for the emir, it is not valid, because that is association (shirk). And if you increase humility, because people see it, it is not valid. This is when you mix one act of worship with another act of worship; how much more so if you mix with it a prohibited matter, such as going ahead of your imam. Indeed, it is not permissible to give zakah to one's parents or children, nor to slaves or maids, because sincerity is not achieved. If you seek by it the joy of your father or your son, sincerity departs; how much more if you seek the pleasure of your desire — how can sincerity remain?

The expressions of the early scholars have differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿sincere﴾:

Some said: acknowledging Him in worship. Others said: intending with their hearts the pleasure of Allah in worship. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, they worship Him, affirming His oneness, not worshipping anything alongside Him. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship one God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿inclining to truth, and to establish prayer and give zakah﴾, there are several opinions regarding it:

The first view: Mujahid said, "Following the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)." For this reason He said: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth; and he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ [An-Nahl: 123]. This interpretation contains a subtle point. It is as if Allah, Glorified is He, knew that imitation (taqlid) dominates human nature, so He did not forbid imitation entirely, nor did He permit relying on imitation entirely. Therefore He mentioned a people whom all of creation unanimously praises, namely Ibrahim and those with him, saying: ﴿There has already been for you an excellent pattern in Abraham and those with him﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 4]. It is as if He, Exalted is He, said: If you must imitate someone in your religion, then imitate Ibrahim, in that he disavowed the idols. This is not surprising, for he disavowed himself when he surrendered himself to the fires, his wealth when he spent it on guests, and his son when he offered him as a sacrifice. Indeed, it is narrated that he heard, "Subbuhun Quddus" (Glorified, Most Holy), and he liked it, and seeing no one, he asked for it to be repeated, and said, "Not without a reward." So he gave away everything he owned. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) appeared to him and said, "It is right for you, since He named you a close friend (khalil). Take your wealth, for I was the one who said it." Rather, he devoted himself to Allah, even to the point of not wanting anything from Jibril, when Jibril said, "As for you, no." So the Truth, Glorified is He, is as if saying: If you are a worshipper, then worship as he worshipped. If you do not give up what is lawful and the doors of the rulers, will you not give up what is forbidden and agreeing with the devils? If you cannot follow Ibrahim, then strive to follow his young son, how he submitted to his Lord's command despite his youth, when he offered his neck to the judgment of the dream. And if you are less than a man, then follow the one described as deficient in intellect, namely the mother of the one sacrificed, how she swallowed that grief. Furthermore, a free woman is half a man, for two women stand in the place of one man in testimony and inheritance; and a slave woman is half a free woman, as evidence that a free woman has two nights in the rotation. Hajar was a quarter of a man. Then consider how she obeyed her Lord, bearing the trial with her children, and then how she was patient when the Friend (Ibrahim) left her alone and isolated in the mountains of Makkah, without water or provisions, and he departed without speaking to her or turning toward her. She said, "Did Allah command you to do this?" He nodded his head, "Yes." So she was content with that and patient through those hardships.

The second view: What is meant by His words ﴿hunafa'﴾ is "upright." Hanaf means uprightness. The one whose foot is bent is called ahnaf only as a figure of optimism, as we say of a blind person "one who sees" and of a deadly desert "a place of safety." A parallel is His words: ﴿Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah" and then remained steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30], and ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [Al-Fatihah: 5].
